comments.body:
ADJACENT INSTANCE, 2026-08-07 — a STATUS clobber with the description INTACT. Recording here because it is the same 'a landed write was silently reverted' class, but the signature differs usefully from this ticket's reported one.

Sequence, all verified by re-reading the ticket after each step:
1. `858c` was closed (a ruling I recorded).
2. The operator refined the ruling, so `rebar reopen 858c` — verified status=open immediately after.
3. Its description was then rewritten with rescoped acceptance criteria — verified landed.
4. Some minutes later, `858c` read back as **closed** again, with the rescoped description and BOTH comments still present and correct.

So the DESCRIPTION write survived and the STATUS write did not. That asymmetry is the useful part: whatever reverted it was not a wholesale revision rollback but a status-only overwrite, which points at inbound field-level reconciliation rather than an event-log or compaction fault. Jira still held the ticket as closed from step 1, so the likely mechanism is an inbound reconcile pass syncing the stale remote status back over the newer local one.

Corroborating sighting the same day, independently reported by another agent: ticket `556a` 'reverted from open to in_progress on its own between two checks (most likely an inbound Jira reconcile)'. Two tickets, two agents, same shape. Note the Reconcile Bridge was re-enabled mid-session, so both fall inside a window where inbound passes were running again.

Re-reopened `858c` and re-verified. If it drifts a third time the mechanism is confirmed and this deserves its own ticket rather than a comment here — the discriminating test would be whether the local STATUS event is still the latest in the event log while the projected state disagrees, which would isolate reducer/projection from inbound overwrite.

comments.body:
Correction / re-attribution for the 858c evidence recorded on this ticket.

The 858c reversion noted here (reopened, then read back `closed` with the rescoped description
and both comments intact) is NOT store reconvergence and is not this ticket's subsystem. It has
been traced to the Jira reconciler and filed as `e6e9-ddbf-223b-4f49` (coal-semiliquid-heifer),
linked `discovered_from` this ticket.

Proof: the reverting event is a genuine inbound write, authored `reconciler` / `env_id:
reconciler`, and it is the LATEST status event in 858c's log
(`1786097878273766164-d80fab3f-4d15-404c-9b20-ef7ec4fbeb27-STATUS.json`). Nothing was rolled
back — a newer overriding event was appended.

The description-survived / status-lost asymmetry that looked anomalous under a store-level
hypothesis is exactly what the reconciler mechanism predicts. The arbitration baseline is
advanced from the pass-START snapshot (`reconcile.py:595` -> `_advance_baselines`,
`:514-531`), so it lags rebar's own outbound push by one pass. A reopen is a revert to a
previous value, so local came back to equal the stale baseline; `_suppressed_by_inbound`
(`outbound_field_diff.py:323-334`, status branch `:389-396`) then read that as "local never
changed", suppressed the outbound status push, and inbound mirrored Jira's stale `Done` back
over local. The description differed from the baseline, so it was pushed normally and survived.

Confirmed in the run logs: pass N (run 31168795002) `key=REB-2500 changed=[description,status]`;
bindings.json at f0fe2ce9d4 still `baseline.status='To Do'`; pass N+1 (run 31169292024)
`key=REB-2500 changed=[description]` followed by the inbound STATUS write.

This does not invalidate this ticket's own store-reconvergence hypothesis for any OTHER evidence
it holds — only the 858c comment should be re-attributed.

comments.author: RebarBotNava
comments.body:
rebar-debug Phase 1 root-cause report (2026-08-10)

Historical event reconstruction for puerile-defensive-nighthawk shows that the verified 14,997-character description event was not deleted, reverted, or hidden by Git. It remained in the log. A later 10,582-character whole-description EDIT became authoritative, followed by a 15,666-character repair. The REVIEW_RESULT sidecar landed about 0.5 ms before the shorter EDIT but did not overwrite the description.

Two mechanisms were tested separately:

1. Historical reducer-cache race — proven and already fixed by commit 0b964c82f5 / closed ticket likeminded-flameproof-tick. Old code let concurrent reducer generations share one .cache.json.tmp; an older reducer could publish a current event hash with stale state. A deterministic regression test passes 5/5 on current origin/main and fails on the parent of that fix by returning old-title while cache-bypassing replay returns new-title. This mechanism can explain a successful immediate read-back followed by a later stale read.

2. Stale-base whole-field overwrite — still reproducible on current origin/main. edit --description appends an unconditional complete replacement, and the reducer applies EDIT fields last-writer-wins. In an isolated repository, after writing fresh-B, a later writer submitted stale client text base-plus-A; both normal reduction and cache-bypassing full replay then returned base-plus-A. This is not caching: it is a newer valid event carrying stale client-held data.

The historical log proves the later writer used older text, but it cannot distinguish whether that stale base came from the now-fixed reducer cache race, a harness retaining old text, or another clone operating inside the documented freshness window. Git caching and filesystem caching are not supported by the evidence: reduction reads current event files, and publication uses atomic rename before the write returns.

Disposition: do not close this as merely a duplicate of the fixed cache ticket. The cache defect is fixed, but stale whole-body writes can still silently clobber newer content. Preventing that requires an explicit API/design decision such as a base revision/fingerprint or field-level compare-and-swap; current optimistic concurrency only covers state-dependent operations, so that behavior should not be changed silently.

compiled_state.description:
## Silent data loss in the store under concurrent write + in-flight review

**Evidence is SECONDHAND** — reported by the session working [rebar:aec1-76e7-bb95-4c86], not
reproduced by the filing session. Filed anyway because it is silent DATA LOSS in the ticket store,
which is the system of record for every agent.

### What was observed

1. A `rebar edit --description` succeeded and was **verified by read-back at 14,997 chars**.
2. A subsequent `rebar show` returned **10,582 chars** — an OLDER revision. Nothing reported an
   error; no conflict, no `ConcurrencyError`, no exit 10.
3. The agent's next read-modify-write then grafted new edits onto that stale text, **corrupting an
   acceptance criterion** by splicing two unrelated fragments:

       - [ ] a gate run persists `finish_reason` (recorded for triage, deliberately not rendered) (the windowed distinct-ratio that
             rebar ticket 70bc establishes is computable from the record)

4. Only a further read-back caught it. The agent rebuilt from a saved good revision and verified
   the restore (15,666 chars, all markers present).

### The reporter's hypothesis (unproven)

The ticket was being edited **while its own `rebar review-plan` was running**, and a review emits
its own `REVIEW_RESULT` sidecar events (`sidecar_emitted: true`). Store reconvergence between the
two writers is the suspected cause. Corroborating signal: a later write to the same ticket with **no
review in flight** stayed intact.

### Why this is worth a ticket rather than a note

* **Optimistic concurrency did not fire.** The documented protection is a `ConcurrencyError`/exit 10
  on a conflicting write. Here the write reported success, verified on read-back, and was then
  silently rolled back — which is the one failure mode the concurrency design is supposed to make
  impossible.
* **Read-back verification is not sufficient**, which invalidates the standard mitigation every
  agent is told to use. The read-back PASSED and the data was still lost afterwards.
* The practical rule that emerged ("never write to a ticket while its own review is running") is an
  undocumented landmine, and it conflicts with the normal remediate-then-review loop the plan-review
  gate asks authors to perform.

## Acceptance Criteria

- [ ] the interaction is REPRODUCED deterministically (concurrent `rebar edit` + an in-flight
      review emitting sidecar events on the same ticket), or the hypothesis is falsified and the
      real trigger identified — the current evidence is a single secondhand observation
- [ ] it is established why optimistic concurrency did not reject the losing write; a silent
      last-writer-wins rollback on a ticket description is either a bug in the conflict detection
      or an undocumented property of sidecar reconvergence
- [ ] a write that will be discarded FAILS LOUDLY (`ConcurrencyError`/exit 10) rather than
      reporting success and reverting afterwards
- [ ] a regression test drives the concurrent-writer path and asserts the losing write is rejected,
      not silently dropped
- [ ] if the 'do not edit during a review' constraint is genuine and must stand, it is DOCUMENTED
      where authors will hit it (the plan-review gate docs describe exactly the revise-then-review
      loop that triggers it)

## Testing

    pytest -m "not integration and not external" -q
